name: Hands in the Manifold
description: A work song that emerged organically from the maintenance tunnels beneath GLMZ's Circuit districts sometime around 2191, its exact authorship disputed across three different unions. Built on a rolling 12/8 polyrhythm drawn from West African dock-work traditions and layered with a low Nordic drone hummed through closed teeth, the song times itself to the rhythm of wrench-turns on pipe fittings — one lyric per rotation. Workers in the thermal conduit crews began singing it first, then electrical maintenance gangs picked it up, then the water reclamation teams, until by 2197 it was functionally the unofficial anthem of every person who worked below street level in the Circuit.
creator: Attributed to the Conduit Workers Local 7 (disputed)
audience: Tier 1 and Tier 2 maintenance workers, tunnel crews, dock laborers, water reclamation teams, infrastructure workers of all kinds
cultural_impact: The song became a labor organizing tool without ever being explicitly political — its verses name specific tools, specific tunnel junctions, specific types of pipe corrosion, making it deeply insider and deeply unifying. When the Circuit Maintenance Strike of 2209 began, workers sang it as they walked off the job in coordinated silence, and the image of thousands of people emerging from maintenance hatches across the city singing the same song was broadcast on pirate feeds for weeks. Vantablack Media's news subsidiaries refused to cover it. The song is now considered the closest thing GLMZ has to a working-class national anthem.
known_fans: pirate radio DJs who play it at shift-change hours
story_hooks: A player character working a maintenance job hears the song being sung around them and realizes the workers are using specific verse choices to communicate covertly — the song's verses map to tunnel junctions and are being used to coordinate something the foreman cannot hear.

A Spire-tier corporate fixer is assigned to discredit the song's origins and prove it was AI-generated propaganda — but the deeper they dig, the more they find evidence it genuinely emerged from the people, and that discovery changes them.

A Tier 5 composer purchases the 'rights' to the song through a legal gray-market claim and releases a polished neural-feed version — the backlash from Circuit workers escalates into something that cannot be contained.
